Vietnam Grapples with Currency Crisis as Dong Plummets, Industry Hit Hard

Vietnam is facing a deepening currency crisis as the Vietnamese dong fell to record lows against the US dollar this week, sparking concerns of broader economic instability. The State Bank of Vietnam intervened on Monday to steady the currency, but the dong remained under pressure, hovering near 26,000 to the dollar in afternoon trading—a depreciation of nearly 12% since the start of the year.

The rapid devaluation has led to surging import costs and mounting inflationary pressures across the country. Industrial firms are reporting immediate impacts. Petroleum Equipment Assembly & Metal Structure JSC, a major supplier to Vietnam’s energy sector, said in a statement Tuesday that volatility in the exchange rate has sharply increased its costs for imported steel and machinery. "We are facing unprecedented challenges in managing contracts and maintaining margins," said Tran Duc Minh, the company’s CFO. "If the situation persists, we may have to review our workforce and investment plans."

The Vietnam Association of Manufacturers warned that the crisis is hampering operations nationwide, citing disruptions in supply chains and a spike in the cost of raw materials. Smaller exporters are particularly vulnerable, with some pausing shipments or renegotiating deals as input costs rise and customers hesitate.

Economists say the crisis is being fueled by global risk aversion, a widening trade deficit, and recent outflows from Vietnam’s financial markets. "Vietnam’s fundamentals remain strong, but the currency shock could undermine confidence if not contained soon," said Nguyen Thi Lan, senior economist at Saigon Policy Institute.

The government has pledged further measures to stabilize markets, but uncertainty remains high as businesses and households brace for more volatility.
